6.3 — Jump Feel: Fall Speed & Coyote Time

Your jump works and your ground check is honest — and the character still feels like it is being operated through a spreadsheet. That is not a vague complaint. "Feel" is four tunable numbers with names, and every platformer you have ever called tight is using all four. Today you learn their names, decide where each number lives, and build the two that are timers.

The Problem: It Works and It Feels Bad ~15 min

Play your cave for thirty seconds and pay attention to your hands, not the screen. Notice three specific complaints — they are the three that every playtester in the world reports, and each one has a name and a fix:

  • "I float down like a balloon." Your rise and your fall use the same gravity. Real characters fall faster than they rise.
  • "I pressed jump right at the edge and nothing happened." Your check turns false the instant your feet leave the ledge, so the game rejects a jump the player genuinely made.
  • "I pressed jump just before landing and nothing happened." The mirror image: the input arrives a few frames before the ground does, and gets thrown away.
The knobThe complaint it killsWhat it really is
Asymmetric gravity (a fall multiplier) "It floats." One gravity number for the rise and a larger one for the fall, chosen by which way the body is currently moving vertically.
Coyote time "The ledge ate my jump." Remember the last moment you were grounded. Keep accepting a jump for a short window after that moment has passed.
Jump buffer "I pressed too early." Remember the last moment the key went down. Fire the jump the instant the ground check goes true, if the press was recent enough.
Variable jump height "I can't do small hops." Release the key early and the rise is cut short. The player's release becomes an input, not just their press.
Both mercies are the same pattern you met in 3.3. A timestamp is written when something happened, and later you compare the clock against it. The fire-rate cooldown said "has enough time passed?". Coyote time and the buffer say "has too much time passed?" — the same subtraction, read in the opposite direction.

Socratic: Forgiving Intent Versus Playing For Them

  1. Coyote time and the jump buffer both let a press count when it "should not". Why does that make the player feel more in control, when technically it makes the game more permissive?
  2. Set coyote time long enough and you can jump from thin air a metre past a ledge. What is the difference between forgiving the player's intent and playing the game for them?
  3. Asymmetric gravity is a lie about physics. Name one other lie your character already tells — and say what each lie buys the player.
  4. Which of the four knobs needs to know which way the body is moving, and which only need to know about time?
  5. Two of these are timers and two are numbers. Does that split tell you anything about where in your script each belongs?
  6. Which of the four would a player notice immediately if you removed it from a game they had been playing for an hour?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Each of these is a timer with a name, from somewhere that is not a video game. Read it for the shape of the logic, then decide which of your four knobs it describes.

Example 1 — A subway door that stays open a moment longer (comment only):

// The doors do not reopen because a hand is in them. They reopen because the
// hand was in them a fraction of a second ago and the timer has not expired.

Example 2 — A parking meter grace period:

bool stillFine = Time.time - paidAt <= gracePeriod; // paid a moment ago, not now

Example 3 — A lift that reopens if you press within a second (comment only):

// The press is remembered, not honoured immediately. The doors are already
// closing; the remembered press is what brings them back.

Example 4 — A wind tunnel ramping down instead of cutting off:

// Falling air is not the same as rising air. The tunnel is symmetric on paper
// and asymmetric in the test chamber, on purpose.

Example 5 — A keyboard's repeat delay:

// Hold the key and the characters start after a pause, then arrive fast.
// The pause is a number somebody chose.

Map Them Before You Build Them

  1. Which example is coyote time, and which is the jump buffer? Be precise — one of them remembers a state and one remembers a press.
  2. The lift example remembers a press that arrives too late. In your game, what is the equivalent of "the doors are already closing"?
  3. The wind tunnel is asymmetric on purpose. Which of your two directions should be the strong one, and what does the player read into that?
  4. The parking meter compares the clock against a past moment. What value do you write down, and what do you compare against it, for each of your two timers?
  5. The keyboard repeat delay is a number somebody chose. Where is that number in your project going to live so that somebody else can choose it?
Build Lab: The Fall Multiplier ~20 min
Architectural specification: asymmetric gravity.
  • What tells you the body is falling? Name the exact quantity you read, and which of its two components matters. (Careful: in Unity 6 that property was renamed. Older tutorials and older Stack Overflow answers will call it something else — find the current name in the docs before you type it.)
  • Which gravity number is "normal"? You already set gravity for the cave in 6.1. Where is that number now — a literal in your own code, a serialized field, or a value you read off the Rigidbody2D? Whatever the answer, you now need it in two places, and that is a design smell worth fixing rather than living with.
  • Your options for the "normal" number: (a) a second serialized field you keep equal to the first by hand, (b) read gravityScale once in Start() and keep it in a private field, (c) a named constant. Which one survives a teammate changing the Inspector value, and which one survives a teammate changing the scene-mode logic you wrote in 6.1?
  • What happens in the top-down Overworld if this logic runs there? Your character has Gravity Scale 0 and never falls, so a "falling" branch may never be true — but the rising branch might be, and it will happily overwrite your 0. Which scene-mode flag from 6.1 gates this?
  • Update() or FixedUpdate()? You are writing a physics property that the physics engine reads. Argue it, then test the other one and describe the difference.
  • Do you also need to restore normal gravity when the body is rising, or only multiply it when falling? What happens on the very first frame after a jump if you only write the falling branch?

Test it the way a player would. Set the multiplier to 1 and play: that is the balloon you started with. Set it to 2.5 and play. Set it to 8 and play. Write one sentence per value. Then go back through the four ways to leave the ground you compared in 6.1 and answer honestly: does this trick work equally well with all four, or does your choice constrain you here?

Build Lab: The Two Mercies ~20 min
Architectural specification: coyote time.
  • What exact moment do you record, and where in your script is the one place the ground check is already computed? Recording it anywhere else means you now have two ground checks and one of them is wrong.
  • What is the comparison that decides "still within the window"? Write it in English first: "if the time since I was last grounded is less than X".
  • How long is the window — 0.05s, 0.1s, 0.2s? Pick a number, then test it by running off a ledge and pressing jump as late as you can.
  • What is the "spend" rule? If you jump using the grace window, can you jump again on the next frame using the same recorded moment? What has to happen to that timestamp at the instant the jump fires?
  • What is the initial value of your timestamp field before the player has ever touched the ground? If it starts at 0 and the game clock starts near 0, what does your first frame of play do?
Architectural specification: jump buffer.
  • Which moment do you record now — and is it the same variable as the coyote one? Two timers, two names, two responsibilities.
  • The jump fires when two things are true: a recent press was remembered and the character is grounded (or inside the coyote window). Write that as a sentence with an AND in it before you write any code.
  • Does the buffer need its own spend rule, or can the same jump fire twice off one remembered press the moment you land and leave the ground again?
  • Your key check from 6.1 was GetKeyDown. Does the buffer replace it or wrap it? Which one is the "input happened" fact and which one is the "input is still relevant" fact?
  • Test it by pressing jump a fraction of a second before you land from a fall. Then press it a full second before. Where is the boundary, and is the boundary the number you thought you set?
Two timers and one jump key is how you build an infinite jump by accident. If the grace window is never spent, a player can tap the key repeatedly in mid-air and every tap lands inside a window that never closes. Watch the Console line you print each time the jump fires — if the count climbs while you are nowhere near the floor, one of your timestamps is being refreshed when it should not be.

Variable jump height is the fourth knob and the smallest change: the rise is a velocity, and the player's release can shorten it. Decide what to cut, when to allow the cut (only while rising? only on the first jump?), and whether it interacts with the jump buffer you just built — a buffered jump the player never held will be cut instantly if you are careless. Test all four knobs together before you move on.

Bug Hunt: The Mushy Jump ~15 min

Bug Hunt

  1. Delete the branch that restores normal gravity while rising, so only the falling case is written. Jump. Where does the character end up, and why does the next full jump leave you barely off the floor?
  2. Never spend the coyote timestamp after a jump. Stand still on the floor and tap the key twice quickly, then walk off a ledge and tap it again. How many jumps did you get, and which single line was supposed to stop that?
  3. Set your coyote window to half a second. Jump from the middle of a gap that is nowhere near a ledge. What did you just build, and what word from 6.2 describes it?
  4. Set the fall multiplier to 10 and land from a full-height jump. Where does the character's feet end up relative to the tile, and what does that tell you about how hard the physics engine is being asked to look?
  5. Run your gravity changes in Update() and then again in FixedUpdate(). On a machine running at 144 frames per second, which one applies the multiplier more often — and why does that make the jump feel different on different computers?
  6. Set the fall multiplier to 0.4 — the fall is now slower than the rise. Play for a minute and describe the genre you accidentally changed your game into.
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Feel Portfolio

  1. Tune a "heavy knight" and a "nimble rogue" — four numbers each. Hand the numbers to another team and have them build the character from paper only. Can they feel which one they built?
  2. What do the four numbers hide when you hand them over? Name the abstraction in one sentence, and name the one thing a teammate cannot recover from the numbers alone.
  3. Make the fall multiplier apply only in the cave. Which scene-mode decision from 6.1 did that force you to look at again, and is it still the right one?
  4. Print the two timestamps every frame for ten seconds and watch them. What does each one do at the exact moment you land, and what does the other one do?
  5. Delete one of the four knobs entirely and play. Which removal is the least noticeable, and which one can you not live without?
  6. Commit and push: "6.3: fall multiplier + coyote + buffer".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain asymmetric gravity and apply it on the physics clock
  • Say where the "normal" gravity number lives, and why that is the right home
  • Build coyote time and the jump buffer from the timestamp pattern in 3.3
  • Explain "spending" a grace window and describe the infinite-jump bug it prevents
  • Defend all four knobs as intent-forgiveness rather than difficulty-lowering
  • Commit and push
